1
刑法志
Treatise on Punishment and Law
2
傳曰：「齊之以禮，有恥且格。 」刑之不可犯，不若禮之不可逾，則昊歲比於犧年，宜有降矣。 若夫穹圓肇判，宵貌攸分，流形播其喜怒，稟氣彰其善惡，則有自然之理焉。 念室後刑，衢樽先惠，將以屏除災害，引導休和，取譬琴瑟，不忘銜策，擬陽秋之成化，若堯舜之為心也。 效原布肅，軒皇有轡野之師； 雷電揚威，高辛有觸山之務。 陳乎兵甲而肆諸市朝，具嚴天刑，以懲亂首，論其本意，蓋有不得已而用之者焉。 是以丹浦興仁，羽山咸服。 而世屬僥倖，事關攸蠹，政失禮微，獄成刑起，則孔子曰：「聽訟吾猶人也，必也使無訟乎！ 」及周氏龔行，卻收鋒刃，祖述生成，憲章堯禹，政有膏露，威兼禮樂，或觀辭以明其趣，或傾耳以照其微，或彰善以激其情，或除惡以崇其本。 至夫取威定霸，一匡九合，寓言成康，不由凝網，此所謂酌其遺美，而愛民治國者焉。 若乃化蔑彝倫，道睽明慎，則夏癸之虔劉百姓，商辛之毒{疒甫}四海，衛鞅之無所自容，韓非之不勝其虐，與夫《甘棠》流詠，未或同歸。 秦文初造參夷，始皇加之抽協，囹圄如市，悲哀盈路。 漢王以三章之法以吊之，文帝以刑厝之道以臨之，于時百姓欣然，將逢交泰。 而犴逐情遷，科隨意往，獻瓊杯于闕下，徙青衣于蜀路，覆醢裁刑，傾宗致獄。 況乃數囚於京兆之夜，五日于長安之市，北闕相引、中都繼及者，亦往往而有焉。 而將亡之國，典刑咸棄，刊章以急其憲，適意以寬其網，桓靈之季，不其然歟！ 魏明帝時，宮室盛興，而期會迫急，有稽限者，帝親召問，言猶在口，身首已分。 王肅抗疏曰：「陛下之所行刑，皆宜死之人也。 然眾庶不知，將為倉卒，願陛下下之于吏而暴其罪。 均其死也，不汙宮掖，不為搢紳驚惋，不為遠近所疑。 人命至重，難生易殺，氣絕而不續者也，是以聖王重之。 孟軻云：'殺一不辜而取天下者，仁者不為也。'」
The Classics record: "Guide the people with ritual, and they will feel shame and set themselves right." Making men fear the executioner is still less worthy than making them shrink from breaching ritual; set beside the halcyon age when even the yearling ox went untouched, our own times can only rank lower. From the primal rending of the round sky into light and darkness, living forms have voiced joy and anger, and the endowment of vital breath has disclosed good and evil—so the world carries an order not imposed from without. Detention was brief before sentence, kindness shown before the rod—meant to banish disaster and lead society toward concord, like tuning strings on a lute yet never laying aside rein and crop, in the spirit of the Spring and Autumn's impartial rule and the humane purpose Yao and Shun held in their hearts. Across the open country he spread solemn terror, and the Yellow Emperor led hosts that bridled the wild plain. Lightning flashed as awe was proclaimed, and Emperor Ku pressed the punitive work against the mountain spirit. Arms were paraded, traitors displayed at market and court, and Heaven's stern penalties fell on the chief rebels—and judged by the purpose behind them, such measures must sometimes have been unavoidable. Thus at Danpu Shun could advance humane rule, and at Yushan even Gun's faction yielded to justice. Yet when the times favor the lucky, worms eat at the foundations, government slackens and ritual grows faint, and packed jails bring punishments in their train, Confucius said, "I can judge a case as well as the next man, but what I want is that there should be no cases to judge." When the Zhou turned from naked force and sheathed the sword, they honored growth and nurture, took Yao and Shun for their charter, and governed with kindness like gentle rain while inspiring fear through ritual and music—now weighing pleas to grasp intent, now listening closely to catch what was hidden, now lifting virtue to stir the heart, now rooting out wickedness to strengthen the moral core. Those who won awe, settled hegemony, and in a single alignment gathered the nine domains, invoking the peace of Kings Cheng and Kang without relying on a mesh of harsh laws, took the best of the old ways and governed in a spirit that truly cherished the people. When moral transformation is cast aside and the Way abandons careful justice, you get Jie of Xia butchering his subjects, Zhou of Shang ravaging the realm, Shang Yang with no refuge from his own doctrine, Han Fei drowning in cruelty—nothing that ends in the same key as the love once sung for the lord of the sweet pear. Duke Wen of Qin first devised kin-extermination; the First Emperor piled on mutilation and dismemberment until jails crowded like marketplaces and wailing filled every road. The King of Han soothed the realm with his three-article code, and Emperor Wen governed with the ideal of idle racks and empty courts; the people rejoiced, believing great peace was at hand. Yet the law ran with passion instead of principle, statutes bent to caprice, bribes in jade reached the palace while innocents in convict dress were driven to Shu; summary justice overturned the pickle-jar precedent, and whole clans were dragged to the cells. Nor were nights that saw multiple heads fall in Jingzhao, or five straight market-days of executions in Chang'an, with the northern gate denunciations pulling in fresh victims and the inner capital echoing the slaughter, anything rare in those years. Dying regimes threw precedent away, rushed edicts to sharpen the code, then relaxed it again on a whim—can anyone doubt that was the face of the reigns of Emperors Huan and Ling? Under Wei Mingdi, palace building ran wild and court schedules turned brutal: anyone who missed a deadline was hauled before the throne, and before he had finished speaking his head rolled. Wang Su remonstrated: "Every man you put to death under these circumstances is indeed guilty of a capital crime." But the people cannot see that and will call it arbitrary killing; I ask that you remand them to the judiciary and publish their offenses." The sentence is the same, yet the harem is not stained with blood, officials need not shudder in secret, and no one near or far is left wondering what really happened." A human life is the weightiest of things: once breath stops it cannot be renewed, though it is easily taken—so the sage kings treated it with utmost care." Mencius said, "No humane ruler would seize the realm at the cost of a single innocent life."
3
世祖武皇帝接三統之微，酌千年之範，乃命有司，大明刑憲。 于時詔書頒新法於天下，海內同軌，人甚安之。 條綱雖設，稱為簡惠，仰昭天眷，下濟民心，道有法而無敗，德俟刑而久立。 及晉圖南徙，百有二年，仰止前規，挹其流潤，江左無外，蠻陬來格。 孝武時，會稽王道子傾弄朝權，其所樹之黨，貨官私獄，烈祖惛迷，不聞司敗，晉之綱紀大亂焉。
Emperor Wu, founding exemplar of our house, gathered the faint line of the Three Ages and weighed a millennium of precedent, then charged his ministers to bring the criminal code into clear order. Edicts spread the new code across the empire; the realm ran on a single gauge, and the people found deep reassurance in it. The framework was in place yet praised as lean and merciful: it reflected Heaven's care above and steadied the people below, so the Way could rely on law without collapsing, and virtue, paired with punishment, could stand the test of time. After the court crossed the Yangzi and held the south for a hundred and two years, it still revered the old statutes and drew on their lingering humanity; beyond the River the land was secure, and outlying peoples offered allegiance. Under Emperor Xiaowu, Prince Daozi of Kuaiji twisted the government; his clique sold posts and ran private jails while Emperor Xiaowu sank into stupor and never listened to the chief judge—so the backbone of the Jin state snapped.
4
傳曰「三皇設言而民不違，五帝畫象而民知禁」，則《書》所謂「象以典刑，流宥五刑，鞭作官刑，撲作教刑」者也。 然則犯黥者皁其巾，犯劓者丹其服，犯臏者墨其體，犯宮者雜其屢，大辟之罪，殊刑之極，布其衣裾而無領緣，投之於市，與眾棄之。 舜命皋陶曰； 「五刑有服，五服三就，五流有宅，五宅三居。 」方乎前載，事既參倍。 夏後氏之王天下也，則五刑之屬三千。 殷因于夏，有所損益。 周人以三典刑邦國，以五聽察民情，左嘉右肺，事均熔造，而五刑之屬猶有二千五百焉。 乃置三刺、三宥、三赦之法：一刺曰訊群臣，再刺曰訊群吏，三刺曰訊萬民； 一宥曰不識，再宥曰過失，三宥曰遺忘； 一赦曰幼弱，再赦曰老旄，三赦曰蠢愚。 《司馬法》：或起甲兵以征不義，廢貢職則討，不朝會則誅，亂嫡庶則縶，變禮刑則放。
The Classics say the Three Sovereigns needed only words to keep the people in line, and the Five Emperors only symbolic pictures to show what was forbidden—that matches the "Document" passage on picturing the five punishments, commuting them with exile, substituting the lash for official faults, and the rod for moral instruction. Branded men wore dark caps, nose-cutters red clothes, kneecap-cutters bore black marks on the flesh, eunuchs odd footwear, and those condemned to death were dressed in collarless, unhemmed cloth and cast before the crowd in the market. Shun charged Gao Yao: "The five punishments each have their proper use, with three places of execution; the five degrees of banishment each have their allotted residence, with three grades of remoteness." Set beside the accounts of high antiquity, the system had already grown several times more elaborate. Under the Xia, offenses classed under the five punishments ran to three thousand articles. The Shang took over the Xia code, trimming and expanding it in places. The Zhou judged the feudal domains with the three codes, sounded popular sentiment with the five hearings, and placed the appeal stones for praise and grievance on either hand, refining justice as in a forge—yet two thousand five hundred offenses still fell under the five punishments. They added three rounds of consultation, three grounds for mitigation, and three classes of mercy: first ask the ministers, then the officials, then the common people; the first mitigation is ignorance of law, the second inadvertent fault, the third lapse of memory; the first amnesty covers the very young, the second the very old, the third the feeble-minded." The Sima fa states that armies marched against injustice, lapsed tribute brought reprisal, skipped audiences meant death, mixed succession led to arrest, and tampering with ritual or penal norms meant exile.
5
傳曰：「殷周之質，不勝其文。 」及昭後徂征，穆王斯耄，爰制刑辟，以詰四方，奸宄弘多，亂離斯永，則所謂「夏有亂政而作《禹刑》，商有亂政而作《湯刑》，周有亂政而作《九刑》」者也。 古者大刑用甲兵，中刑用刀鋸，薄刑用鞭撲。 自茲厥後，狙詐彌繁。 武皇帝並以為往憲猶疑，不可經國，乃命車騎將軍、守尚書令、魯公徵求英俊，刊律定篇云爾。
The Classics remark that the plain vigor of Shang and Zhou could not match their growing refinement." When King Zhao marched far afield and King Mu turned old, new statutes were forged to cow the regions; knavery multiplied and turmoil dragged on—that is the sense of "The Xia wrote the Yu code in an age of chaos, the Shang the Tang code, the Zhou the Nine Punishments." In high antiquity the gravest crimes were punished with war, middling ones with the blade, light ones with lash or stick. Thereafter guile multiplied and the law multiplied with it. Our Emperor Wu judged the inherited code too ambiguous for running the realm and ordered the chariot general, provisional chief of the Secretariat, the Duke of Lu, to gather able scholars, edit the statutes, and settle the final text—and so it was done.
6
漢自王莽篡位之後，舊章不存。 光武中興，留心庶獄，常臨朝聽訟，躬決疑事。 是時承離亂之後，法網弛縱，罪名既輕，無以懲肅。 梁統乃上疏曰：
Once Wang Mang seized the Han throne, the former legal order vanished. Emperor Guangwu, reviving Han, took a close interest in justice, regularly held audience to hear cases, and settled doubtful points himself. Coming after civil war, the law hung loose, penalties were mild, and there was little to inspire fear. Liang Tong therefore presented a memorial:
7
臣竊見元帝初元五年，輕殊刑三十四事，哀帝建平元年盡四年，輕殊死者刑八十一事，其四十二事，手殺人皆減死罪一等，著為常法。 自是以後，人輕犯法，吏易殺人，吏民俱失，至於不羈。
I note that in 44 BCE thirty-four provisions softened the death penalty, and between 4 and 1 BCE eighty-one more did the same; forty-two of those, all involving homicide with one's own hand, commuted capital sentences by one grade and were fixed as permanent rules. After that, subjects flouted the law and magistrates killed casually; ruler and ruled alike lost their bearings until restraint broke down entirely.
8
臣愚以為刑罰不苟務輕，務其中也。 君人之道，仁義為主，仁者愛人，義者理務。 愛人故當為除害，理務亦當為去亂。 是以五帝有流殛放殺之誅，三王有大辟刻肌之刑，所以為除殘去亂也。 故孔子稱「仁者必有勇」，又曰「理財正辭，禁人為非曰義」。 高帝受命，制約令，定法律，傳之後世，可常施行。 文帝寬惠溫克，遭世康平，因時施恩，省去肉刑，除相坐之法，他皆率由舊章，天下幾致升平。 武帝值中國隆盛，財力有餘，出兵命將，征伐遠方，軍役數興，百姓罷弊，豪傑犯禁，奸吏弄法，故設遁匿之科，著知縱之律。 宣帝聰明正直，履道握要，以禦海內，臣下奉憲，不失繩墨。 元帝法律，少所改更，天下稱安。 孝成、孝哀，承平繼體，即位日淺，聽斷尚寡。 丞相王嘉等猥以數年之間，虧除先帝舊約，穿令斷律，凡百餘事，或不便於政，或不厭人心。 臣謹表取其尤妨政事、害善良者，傅奏如左。
I submit that the goal of punishment is not to be as lenient as possible, but to strike the right balance. A ruler's path rests on humanity and right: the humane man cherishes his people, the righteous man sets affairs in order. To love the people is to rid them of injury; to set affairs straight is to purge chaos. Hence the Five Emperors used exile and death, and the Three Dynasties added dismemberment and the axe—all to extirpate violence and end turmoil. Confucius therefore said the humane must also be brave, and defined righteousness as straightening finance, correcting speech, and stopping wrong before it starts. Gaozu took Heaven's charge, issued his compact statutes, and set the code that later reigns were to follow without caprice. Emperor Wen, gentle and temperate, ruled a tranquil world: he remitted mutilation, ended guilt by kin, and left the rest of Gaozu's code intact—so that the empire nearly touched the heights of peace. Emperor Wu found a rich, strong China and sent armies far abroad; constant levies wore the people down, outlaws multiplied, and corrupt clerks twisted the law—so he added articles on fugitives and on officials who knowingly let criminals go. Emperor Xuan, clear-sighted and just, held the essentials and kept the realm in hand; his officials enforced the code straight as a plumb line. Emperor Yuan changed little in the statutes, and the country was reckoned secure. Cheng and Ai, taking peaceful succession early in their reigns, had heard comparatively few cases. Within a few years Chancellor Wang Jia and his colleagues wantonly repealed the late emperor's agreements, hacked at statutes, and pushed through over a hundred changes—some harmful to government, some hateful to the people. I have singled out the measures that most cripple the administration and wrong honest men, and list them below.
9
伏惟陛下苞五常，履九德，推時撥亂，博施濟時，而反因循季世末節，衰微軌跡，誠非所以還初反本，據元更始也。 願陛下宣詔有司，悉舉初元、建平之所穿鑿，考其輕重，察其化俗，足以知政教所處，擇其善者而從之，其不善者而改之，定不易之典，施之無窮，天下幸甚。
You embody the Five Constants and walk the Nine Virtues, set the age to rights and relieve distress—yet you cling to the dregs of a dying era; that cannot be how you return to first principles and begin anew from the root. Order your ministers to collect every Jianping and Chuyuan innovation, weigh each for severity and effect on the people, keep what helped right rule, discard what harmed it, and promulgate a stable code for all time—the empire will be the gainer.
10
至章帝時，尚書陳寵上疏曰：「先王之政，賞不僭，刑不濫，與其不得已，寧僭不濫。 故唐堯著典曰'流宥五刑，眚災肆赦'。 帝舜命皋陶以'五宅三居，惟明克允'。 文王重《易》六爻，而列叢棘之聽； 周公作《立政》，戒成王勿誤乎庶獄。 陛下即位，率由此義，而有司執事，未悉奉承。 斷獄者急於榜格酷烈之痛，執憲者繁於詐欺放濫之文，違本離實，棰楚為奸，或因公行私，以逞威福。 夫為政也，猶張琴瑟，大弦急者小弦絕，故子貢非臧孫之猛法，而美鄭僑之仁政。 方今聖德充塞，假於上下，宜因此時，隆先聖之務，蕩滌煩苛，輕薄棰楚，以濟群生，廣至德也。 」帝納寵言，決罪行刑，務于寬厚。 其後遂詔有司，禁絕鑽钅贊諸酷痛舊制，解祅惡之禁，除文致之請，讞五十餘事，定著於令。 是後獄法和平。
Under Emperor Zhang, Chen Chong of the Secretariat wrote: "Ancient kings neither lavished rewards nor abused the lash; where they had to err, they preferred excess in mercy to excess in cruelty." Hence Tang Yao's canon reads, "Commute the five punishments with exile; forgive crimes born of misfortune." Shun told Gao Yao that banishment had three degrees of distance, and only a clear judge could apply it faithfully." King Wen deepened the Zhou "Changes" to six lines and held court among the briars; The Duke of Zhou, in "Establishing the Government," warned King Cheng never to mishandle justice. Your Majesty has ruled in that spirit, yet many who hold office have not followed suit. Judges race to rack and scourge; drafters bury the law in quibbles and bogus mercy; they abandon substance for torture, turn the rod into a tool of malice, and hide private spite behind the seal." Government is like a lute: wrench the bass strings and the treble snap; hence Zigong blamed Zangsun's cruelty and praised Zichan's humane rule." Today your sacred virtue fills heaven and earth; this is the hour to revive the sages' work, strip away cruel technicalities, ease the rod, and bring boundless grace to the people. The throne took Chen Chong's advice and leaned toward mercy in sentencing. He then banned the old tortures of awl and brand, repealed laws against "unnatural" omens, struck pleadings that twisted wording to trap the accused, and codified over fifty rules on doubtful cases. From then on justice ran more calmly.
11
永元六年，寵又代郭躬為廷尉，復校律令，刑法溢于《甫刑》者，奏除之，曰：「臣聞禮經三百，威儀三千，故《甫刑》大辟二百，五刑之屬三千。 禮之所去，刑之所取，失禮即入刑，相為表裏者也。 今律令，犯罪應死刑者六百一十，耐罪千六百九十八，贖罪以下二千六百八十一，溢于《甫刑》千九百八十九，其四百一十大辟，千五百耐罪，七十九贖罪。 《春秋保乾圖》曰：'王者三百年一蠲法。 '漢興以來，三百二年，憲令稍增，科條無限。 又律有三家，說各駁異。 刑法繁多，宜令三公、廷尉集平律令，應經合義可施行者，大辟二百，耐罪、贖罪二千八百，合為三千，與禮相應。 其餘千九百八十九事，悉可詳除。 使百姓改易視聽，以成大化，致刑措之美，傳之無窮。 」未及施行，會寵抵罪，遂寢。 寵子忠。 忠後復為尚書，略依寵意，奏上三十三條，為《決事比》，以省請讞之弊。 又上除蠶室刑，解贓吏三世禁錮，狂易殺人得減重論，母子兄弟相代死聽赦所代者，事皆施行。 雖時有蠲革，而舊律繁蕪，未經纂集。
In AD 94 Chen Chong succeeded Guo Gong as commandant of justice, reviewed the code, and asked to cut anything that overshot the Fu xing model: "The rites number three hundred, ceremony three thousand; the Fu code allowed two hundred capital crimes and three thousand offenses under the five punishments." What ritual rejects, law embraces; breach of decorum becomes a penal case—the two are the warp and weft of rule." Today's code lists 610 capital offenses, 1,698 beard-shaving and convict-labor crimes, and 2,681 lesser offenses punishable by fine—1,989 more than the Fu model: 410 of them capital, 1,500 mutilating labor, 79 redeemable." The apocryphal Spring and Autumn chart says a true king purges obsolete statutes once every three centuries. The Han has now stood 302 years; edicts and clauses have piled up without end. Three schools of jurisprudence read the same text three different ways." Let the three dukes and the commandant of justice collate the code: keep 200 capital crimes and 2,800 labor or fine offenses—3,000 items in all—aligned with the rites." The other 1,989 articles should be struck after review." So the people will see justice anew, great reform will be completed, we may approach the ideal of empty prisons, and the example will endure forever." Before the reform took effect Chen Chong fell under accusation and the plan was shelved. Chen Chong was succeeded by his son Chen Zhong. Chen Zhong later returned to the Secretariat, followed his father's aims, presented thirty-three rules as binding precedents, and cut back abuse of appeals for rehearing. He also won abolition of castration, lifted the three-generation disqualification for corrupt clerks, allowed reduced sentences for insane killers, and permitted pardon when kin volunteered to die in a convict's place—each measure was adopted. Piecemeal fixes followed, but the old code stayed a jungle and was never fully codified.
12
獻帝建安元年，應劭又刪定律令，以為《漢議》，表奏之曰：「夫國之大事，莫尚載籍。 載籍也者，決嫌疑，明是非，賞刑之宜，允執厥中，俾後之人永有鑒焉。 故膠東相董仲舒老病致仕，朝廷每有政議，數遣廷尉張湯親至陋巷，問其得失，於是作《春秋折獄》二百三十二事，動以《經》對，言之詳矣。 逆臣董卓，蕩覆王室，典憲焚燎，靡有孑遺，開闢以來，莫或茲酷。 今大駕東邁，巡省許都，拔出險難，其命惟新。 臣竊不自揆，輒撰具《律本章句》、《尚書舊事》、《廷尉板令》、《決事比例》、《司徒都目》、《五曹詔書》及《春秋折獄》，凡二百五十篇，蠲去復重，為之節文。 又集《議駁》三十篇，以類相從，凡八十二事。 其見《漢書》二十五，《漢記》四，皆刪敘潤色，以全本體。 其二十六，博采古今瑰瑋之士，德義可觀。 其二十七，臣所創造。 《左氏》云：'雖有姬薑，不棄憔悴； 雖有絲麻，不棄菅蒯。 '蓋所以代匱也。 是用敢露頑才，廁於明哲之末，雖未足綱紀國體，宣洽時雍。 庶幾觀察，增闡聖德。 惟因萬機之餘暇，遊意省覽。 」獻帝善之，於是舊事存焉。 是時天下將亂，百姓有土崩之勢，刑罰不足以懲惡，於是名儒大才故遼東太守崔實、大司農鄭玄、大鴻臚陳紀之徒，咸以為宜復行肉刑。 漢朝既不議其事，故無所用矣。
In AD 196 Ying Shao revised the law into the Han yi and presented it: "No state business ranks above the written record." Records settle doubts, show truth from falsehood, fix the scale of reward and penalty, hold the golden mean, and hand posterity a clear mirror." When Dong Zhongshu retired ill to Jiaodong, the court often sent Zhang Tang to his door for legal advice; from this came 232 Spring and Autumn case rulings grounded in the classics, set out at length." The traitor Dong Zhuo then toppled the dynasty and burned the archives until nothing survived—no cruelty like it since history began." The imperial train has turned east to Xudu, escaped deadly peril, and received a fresh mandate." I have ventured to compile the statutory gloss, archival precedents, commandant's board rules, case ratios, education ministry indexes, five-bureau edicts, and the Spring and Autumn judgments—250 fascicles in all—stripping overlap and setting the text in order. I have also assembled thirty chapters of collected rebuttals, grouped by topic, covering eighty-two points. Twenty-five passages taken from the Book of Han and four from the Han Records were cut, restated, and polished to keep the whole work intact. Part twenty-six draws widely on remarkable men of every era whose moral conduct repays study. The twenty-seventh section is my own composition. The Zuo Commentary says: 'Even with noble wives at hand, the worn and weary are not abandoned;' even when silk and hemp are plentiful, coarse rushes and reeds are not thrown away. That is how one substitutes for want. So I venture to set my modest talent beside the sages, not to frame the polity or perfect the age, yet perhaps a reader may find in it matter that clarifies royal virtue. I beg that when the myriad tasks allow a breath, Your Majesty glance through these pages. The emperor approved, and the old materials were kept. As the empire slid toward disorder and the people teetered like crumbling earth, the law could no longer curb crime; leading scholars—former Liaodong governor Cui Shi, minister of agriculture Zheng Xuan, grand herald Chen Ji, and others—argued that mutilating penalties should return. The Han never settled the question, so nothing came of it.
13
及魏武帝匡輔漢室，尚書令荀彧博訪百官，復欲申之，而少府孔融議以為：「古者敦厖，善否區別，吏端刑清政簡，一無過失，百姓有罪，皆自取之。 末世陵遲，風化壞亂，政撓其俗，法害其教。 故曰'上失其道，人散久矣'。 而欲繩之以古刑，投之以殘棄，非所謂與時消息也。 紂斮朝涉之脛，天下謂為無道。 夫九牧之地，千八百君，若各刖一人，是天下常有千八百紂也，求世休和，弗可得已。 且被刑之人，慮不念生，志在思死，類多趨惡，莫復歸正。 夙沙亂齊，伊戾禍宋，趙高、英布，為世大患。 不能止人遂為非也，適足絕人還為善耳。 雖忠如鬻拳，信如卞和，智如孫臏，冤如巷伯，才如史遷，達如子政，一罹刀鋸，沒世不齒。 是太甲之思庸，穆公之霸秦，陳湯之都賴，魏尚之臨邊，無所復施也。 漢開改惡之路，凡為此也。 故明德之君，遠度深惟，棄短就長，不苟革其政者也。 」朝廷善之，卒不改焉。
While Cao Cao was restoring Han, chief secretary Xun Yu polled the bureaucracy to revive corporal punishment, but Kong Rong objected: 'In ancient times society was simple, good and evil were plain, officials were honest, the code was lucid, and government was lean; when commoners erred, they had only themselves to blame. In a decadent age morals fray, policy warps the people, and statutes undermine teaching. Hence the saying, "When those above lose the Way, the people scatter for good." To tie them now to ancient mutilation and cast them among the ruined and despised is hardly "moving with the times." When King Zhou of Shang cut the legs of those wading the morning ford, all under Heaven called him lawless. Across the nine provinces stood some eighteen hundred lords; had each ordered one mutilation, the world would have held eighteen hundred King Zhous—peace would have been impossible. Moreover, the branded cease to cherish life; they turn toward death and, for the most part, rush into crime rather than reform. Susha threw Qi into chaos, Yili ruined Song, Zhao Gao and Ying Bu became scourges of their times. They did not keep men from wrongdoing; they only blocked the way back to goodness. Loyal Yu Quan, faithful Bian He, brilliant Sun Bin, the slandered eunuch of "Lane," genius Sima Qian, and discerning Liu Xiang—once the blade fell, they were shut out of decent company forever. So much for Taijia's return to duty, Duke Mu's hegemony, Chen Tang's frontier fame, or Wei Shang's border service—none of that could happen again under such a system. The Han left open a path from crime to reform; that was the whole point. A wise sovereign looks far ahead, discards short-term cruelty for lasting good, and does not change policy on a whim. The court praised Kong Rong's argument and dropped the proposal.
14
及魏國建，陳紀子群時為御史中丞，魏武帝下令又欲復之，使群申其父論。 群深陳其便。 時鐘繇為相國，亦贊成之，而奉常王脩不同其議。 魏武帝亦難以籓國改漢朝之制，遂寢不行。 於是乃定甲子科，犯釱左右趾者易以木械，是時乏鐵，故易以木焉。 又嫌漢律太重，故令依律論者聽得科半，使從半減也。
When the Wei kingdom was founded, Chen Qun—Chen Ji's son—was censor-in-chief; Cao Cao ordered him to restate his father's case for corporal punishment. Chen Qun argued forcefully in its favor. Zhong Yao, as minister of state, concurred, but chamberlain Wang Xiu dissented. Cao Cao, still nominally serving Han, hesitated to overturn Han law from a princely fief, and the plan lapsed. They promulgated the Jiazi statutes: metal toe-fetters gave way to wooden stocks because iron was short. Finding Han penalties harsh, they allowed sentences computed under the code to be halved in practice.
15
魏文帝受禪，又議肉刑。 詳議未定，會有軍事，復寢。 時有大女劉硃，撾子婦酷暴，前後三婦自殺，論硃減死輸作尚方，因是下怨毒殺人減死之令。 魏明帝改士庶罰金之令，男聽以罰金，婦人加笞還從鞭督之例，以其形體裸露故也。
When Cao Pi took the throne, corporal punishment was debated again. Deliberation was still unfinished when war intervened, and the matter was shelved. A woman named Liu Zhu so tormented three successive daughters-in-law that they killed themselves; she was spared execution and sent to the imperial workshops, prompting a statute commuting death for spite-murder. Wei Mingdi revised the fine code: men could redeem with cash, but women were caned instead, lest public flogging leave them stripped.
16
是時承用秦漢舊律，其文起自魏文侯師李悝。 悝撰次諸國法，著《法經》。 以為王者之政，莫急於盜賊，故其律始于《盜賊》。 盜賊須劾捕，故著《網捕》二篇。 其輕狡、越城、博戲、借假不廉、淫侈逾制以為《雜律》一篇，又以《具律》具其加減。 是故所著六篇而已，然皆罪名之制也。 商君受之以相秦。 漢承秦制，蕭何定律，除參夷連坐之罪，增部主見知之條，益事律《興》、《廄》、《戶》三篇，合為九篇。 叔孫通益律所不及，傍章十八篇。 張湯《越宮律》二十七篇。 趙禹《朝律》六篇。 合六十篇。 又漢時決事，集為《令甲》以下三百餘篇，及司徒鮑公撰嫁娶辭訟決為《法比都目》，凡九百六卷。 世有增損，率皆集類為篇，結事為章。 一章之中或事過數十，事類雖同，輕重乖異。 而通條連句，上下相蒙，雖大體異篇，實相采入。 《盜律》有賊傷之例，《賊律》有盜章之文，《興律》有上獄之法，《廄律》有逮捕之事，若此之比，錯糅無常。 後人生意，各為章句。 叔孫宣、郭令卿、馬融、鄭玄諸儒章句十有餘家，家數十萬言。 凡斷罪所當由用者，合二萬六千二百七十二條，七百七十三萬二千二百餘言，言數益繁，覽者益難。 天子於是下詔，但用鄭氏章句，不得雜用餘家。
The code in force still followed Qin and Han precedents; its roots lay in Li Kui, adviser to Marquis Wen of Wei. Li Kui collated the laws of the states and compiled the Fajing. He held that for a king nothing mattered more than theft and banditry, so his code opened with "Robbers and Thieves." Banditry required indictment and arrest, so he added two chapters on nets and pursuit. Light crime, wall-scaling, gaming, dishonest loans, and lavish excess beyond sumptuary rules went into a "Miscellaneous" chapter, while a "General Part" handled aggravation and mitigation. Thus the whole code ran to just six chapters, all defining offenses. Shang Yang took this model to Qin as chief minister. Han adopted Qin law; Xiao He codified it, dropped mass execution and kin liability, added rules on a superior's knowledge of a subordinate's crime, and appended three "affair" chapters—levies, stables, and household—for nine chapters in all. Shusun Tong filled gaps with eighteen supplementary chapters. Zhang Tang contributed twenty-seven chapters of palace regulations. Zhao Yu added six chapters of court law. Together these made sixty chapters. Han case law swelled past three hundred fascicles from Ling jia onward, and Minister Bao compiled marriage and suit precedents into nine hundred sixty rolls of comparative headings. Each reign added or trimmed; over time material was grouped by topic into chapters and clauses. A single chapter could list dozens of unrelated items; though nominally one class, penalties varied wildly. Cross-referenced clauses overlapped so that even separate chapters silently imported one another's rules. Robbery statutes hid assault rules, banditry statutes held theft language, corvée chapters tucked in jail procedures, stable law carried arrest clauses—everything was cross-wired. Later jurists spun private glosses on every line. Ten schools—Shusun Xuan, Guo Lingqing, Ma Rong, Zheng Xuan, and others—each produced hundreds of thousands of words of commentary. Active precedent ran to 26,272 clauses and over 7.32 million words—each revision thicker, each code harder to use. The emperor then decreed exclusive use of Zheng Xuan's commentary, banning rival schools.
17
衛覬又奏曰：「刑法者，國家之所貴重，而私議之所輕賤； 獄吏者，百姓之所懸命，而選用者之所卑下。 王政之弊，未必不由此也。 請置律博士，轉相教授。 」事遂施行。 然而律文煩廣，事比眾多，離本依末，決獄之吏如廷尉獄吏范洪受囚絹二丈，附輕法論之，獄吏劉象受屬偏考囚張茂物故，附重法論之。 洪、象雖皆棄市，而輕枉者相繼。 是時太傅鐘繇又上疏求復肉刑，詔下其奏，司徒王朗議又不同。 時議者百餘人，與朗同者多。 帝以吳蜀未平，又寢。 其後，天子又下詔改定刑制，命司空陳群、散騎常侍劉邵、給事黃門侍郎韓遜、議郎庾嶷、中郎黃休、荀詵等刪約舊科，傍采漢律，定為魏法，制《新律》十八篇，《州郡令》四十五篇，《尚書官令》、《軍中令》，合百八十餘篇。 其序略曰：
Wei Ji submitted: "Criminal law is the state's most solemn business, yet private opinion treats it lightly;' jailors hold the people's lives in their hands, yet the post draws the meanest talent;' Many a failing throne owes something to that mismatch. I ask that chairs of jurisprudence be founded and the code taught in rotation. The throne approved and carried it out. Yet the code sprawled and precedent multiplied; clerks abandoned principle for detail—Fan Hong of the commandant's jail took two bolts of silk from a convict and cited a lenient clause, while Liu Xiang took a bribe, tortured Zhang Mao to death, then cited a harsh clause. Both clerks were executed in the market, yet wrongful sentencing went on as before. Grand tutor Zhong Yao again urged corporal punishment; the emperor referred the memorial to Wang Lang, who disagreed. Over a hundred officials joined the debate, most siding with Wang Lang. The ruler, with Shu and Wu still unconquered, shelved the idea again. Later an edict charged Chen Qun, Liu Shao, Han Xun, Yu Yi, Huang Xiu, Xun Shen, and others to trim old statutes, borrow Han rules, and codify Wei law: eighteen chapters of New Code, forty-five of commandery and prefect orders, plus secretariat and camp regulations—over 180 chapters in all. Their preface ran in substance as follows:'
18
舊律所難知者，由於六篇篇少故也。 篇少則文荒，文荒則事寡，事寡則罪漏。 是以後人稍增，更與本體相離。 今制新律，宜都總事類，多其篇條。
The old code was obscure because six chapters were too few. Few chapters meant thin text, thin text meant missed offenses, missed offenses meant loopholes. Later editors kept adding material until the code drifted from its roots. The new code should reorganize matter by type and expand the number of chapters and clauses.
19
舊律因秦《法經》，就增三篇，而《具律》不移，因在第六。 罪條例既不在始，又不在終，非篇章之義。 故集罪例以為《刑名》，冠於律首。
Wei inherited Qin's Fajing, added three chapters, but left the general part sixth instead of first. Offense definitions sat neither at the head nor the tail—illogical for a code. They therefore compiled general rules as "Names of Punishments" and placed them at the opening of the code.
20
《盜律》有劫略、恐猲、和賣買人，科有持質，皆非盜事，故分以為《劫略律》。 《賊律》有欺謾、詐偽、逾封、矯制、《囚律》有詐偽生死，《令丙》有詐自復免，事類眾多，故分為《詐律》。 《賊律》有賊伐樹木、殺傷人畜產及諸亡印，《金布律》有毀傷亡失縣官財物，故分為《毀亡律》。 《囚律》有告劾、傳覆，《廄律》有告反逮受，科有登聞道辭，故分為《告劾律》。 《囚律》有系囚、鞫獄、斷獄之法，《興律》有上獄之事，科有考事報讞，宜別為篇，故分為《系訊》、《斷獄律》。 《盜律》有受所監受財枉法，《雜律》有假借不廉，《令乙》有呵人受錢，科有使者驗賂，其事相類，故分為《請賕律》。 《盜律》有勃辱強賊，《興律》有擅興徭役，《具律》有出賣呈，科有擅作修舍事，故分為《興擅律》。 《興律》有乏徭稽留，《賊律》有儲峙不辨，《廄律》有乏軍之興，及舊典有奉詔不謹、不承用詔書，漢氏施行有小愆之反不如令，輒劾以不承用詔書乏軍要斬，又減以《丁酉詔書》，《丁酉詔書》，漢文所下，不宜復以為法，故別為之《留律》。 秦世舊有廄置、乘傳、副車、食廚，漢初承秦不改，後以費廣稍省，故後漢但設騎置而無車馬，則律猶著其文，則為虛設，故除《廄律》，取其可用合科者，以為《郵驛令》。 其告反逮驗，別入《告劾律》。 上言變事，以為《變事令》，以驚事告急，與《興律》烽燧及科令者，以為《驚事律》。 《盜律》有還贓畀主，《金布律》有罰贖入責以呈黃金為價，科有平庸坐贓事，以為《償贓律》。 律之初制，無免坐之文，張湯、趙禹始作監臨部主、見知故縱之例。 其見知而故不舉劾，各與同罪，失不舉劾，各以贖論，其不見不知，不坐也，是以文約而例通。 科之為制，每條有違科，不覺不知，從坐之免，不復分別，而免坐繁多，宜總為免例，以省科文，故更制定其由例，以為《免坐律》。 諸律令中有其教制，本條無從坐之文者，皆從此取法也。 凡所定增十三篇，就故五篇，合十八篇，於正律九篇為增，于旁章科令為省矣。
Robbery statutes had mixed in kidnapping, extortion, and human trafficking—none of it simple theft—so a separate "Robbery and Capture" chapter was split off. Banditry chapters lumped fraud, forged orders, and bogus death reports with ordinary crime—so a dedicated "Fraud" statute was carved out. Statutes on banditry had covered timber theft, harm to persons or herds, and lost seals, while treasury rules covered damage to state property—now split into a "Destruction and Loss" chapter. Prison law had held denunciation, transfer, and review alongside stable law's treason arrests—now separated as "Impeachment." Jail procedures, trials, and appeals had been scattered across prison and corvée chapters—now "Detention and Interrogation" and "Trial Judgment" stood on their own. Bribery of overseers, dishonest loans, verbal shakedowns, and envoy extortion were merged into a "Soliciting Bribes" chapter. Robbery statutes had covered humiliation of robbers, corvée law arbitrary levies, and catch-all clauses on illicit building—all combined now as "Unauthorized Acts and Levies." Corvée delay, failure to stock supplies, military shortfall, and Han precedents that equated minor disobedience with capital "failure to execute edicts"—even when mitigated by Emperor Wen's Dingyou edict—were pulled into a new "Delay and Shortfall" chapter instead of borrowing obsolete Han language. Qin-Han post-horse rules lingered as dead letter once Later Han cut chariots; the stable chapter was deleted and surviving useful clauses became a "Post and Relay" ordinance. Denunciation and treason arrest went entirely into "Impeachment." Reports of insurrection became a "Mutiny" order; urgent alarms and beacon rules formed an "Emergency" order. Return of stolen goods, gold-based fines, and valuation of illicit gains were unified under "Restitution of Booty." The original code lacked rules on who escaped joint liability; Zhang Tang and Zhao Yu introduced liability for supervising officials who knowingly let crime pass. Knowing accomplices who failed to report shared guilt; negligent non-reporters paid fines; the truly ignorant went free—so wording stayed lean while coverage stayed broad. Statute chapters piled redundant "unknowing" exemptions; these were consolidated into a single "Exemption from Joint Liability" chapter to shorten the code. Whenever a chapter lacked explicit joint-liability language, courts fell back on the new exemption rules. Thirteen new chapters plus five old heads made eighteen—more than the Han core nine, yet slimmer than the sprawl of side statutes and edicts.
21
改漢舊律不行于魏者皆除之，更依古義制為五刑。 其死刑有三，髡刑有四，完刑、作刑各三，贖刑十一，罰金六，雜抵罪七，凡三十七名，以為律首。 又改《賊律》，但以言語及犯宗廟園陵，謂之大逆無道，要斬，家屬從坐，不及祖父母、孫。 至於謀反大逆，臨時捕之，或汙瀦，或梟菹，夷其三族，不在律令，所以嚴絕惡跡也。 賊鬥殺人，以劾而亡，許依古義，聽子弟得追殺之。 會赦及過誤相殺，不得報仇，所以止殺害也。 正殺繼母，與親母同，防繼假之隙也。 除異子之科，使父子無異財也。 歐兄姊加至五歲刑，以明教化也。 囚徒誣告人反，罪及親屬，異于善人，所以累之使省刑息誣也。 改投書棄市之科，所以輕刑也。 正篡囚棄市之罪，斷凶強為義之蹤也。 二歲刑以上，除以家人乞鞫之制，省所煩獄也。 改諸郡不得自擇伏日，所以齊風俗也。
Han rules Wei did not use were struck, and penalties were reorganized under the classical five punishments. The schedule listed three capital grades, four shaving penalties, three full-status labor grades, three convict-labor grades, eleven redeemable offenses, six money fines, and seven miscellaneous labor offsets—thirty-seven named penalties opening the code. The banditry chapter was tightened: only slanderous language or sacrilege against imperial shrines and tombs counted as "great treason without the Way," punished by waist-cutting with kin liability stopping short of grandparents and grandchildren. Plotting rebellion was handled ad hoc—drowning, exposure, mincing, three-kin extermination—left outside written law to mark its extremity. In affray homicide, if the killer fled indictment, the law allowed sons and brothers to hunt him down under old precedent. Amnesty or accidental killing closed the door to blood feud, checking endless slaughter. Willful murder of a stepmother was equated with killing one's birth mother, closing the gap between stepfamily feints and true kinship. They repealed the rule that split father and son into separate households so family property could stay undivided. Assault on elder siblings was raised to five years' penal labor to underscore moral instruction. If a convict framed someone for treason, his relatives shared liability—unlike honest men—so the law discouraged perjury by threatening kin. The old death penalty for anonymous denunciations was commuted to market exposure, easing the penalty. They fixed the statute on pretended "righteous" seizure of prisoners, blocking thugs who masked robbery as justice. For sentences of two years or more, they abolished the rule letting kin petition for retrial, cutting jailhouse paperwork. Prefectures could no longer pick their own "dog days" for summer trials, so practice was uniform across the realm.
22
斯皆魏世所改，其大略如是。 其後正始之間，天下無事，於是征西將軍夏侯玄、河南尹李勝、中領軍曹羲、尚書丁謐又追議肉刑，卒不能決。 其文甚多，不載。
Such were the Wei-era revisions in broad outline. Later, during the calm Zhengshi years (240–249), Xiahou Xuan, Li Sheng, Cao Xi, and Ding Mi reopened debate on corporal punishment but never reached a verdict. Their memorials ran too long to include.
23
及景帝輔政，是時魏法，犯大逆者誅及已出之女。 毋丘儉之誅，其子甸妻荀氏應坐死，其族兄顗與景帝姻，通表魏帝，以匄其命。 詔聽離婚。 荀氏所生女芝，為潁川太守劉子元妻，亦坐死，以懷妊系獄。 荀氏辭詣司隸校尉何曾乞恩，求沒為官婢，以贖芝命。 曾哀之，使主簿程咸上議曰：「夫司寇作典，建三等之制； 甫侯修刑，通輕重之法。 叔世多變，秦立重辟，漢又修之。 大魏承秦漢之弊，未及革制，所以追戮已出之女，誠欲殄丑類之族也。 然則法貴得中，刑慎過制。 臣以為女人有三從之義，無自專之道，出適他族，還喪父母，降其服紀，所以明外成之節，異在室之恩。 而父母有罪，追刑已出之女； 夫黨見誅，又有隨姓之戮。 一人之身，內外受辟。 今女既嫁，則為異姓之妻； 如或產育，則為他族之母，此為元惡之所忽。 戮無辜之所重，於防則不足懲奸亂之源，於情則傷孝子之心。 男不得罪於他族，而女獨嬰戮於二門，非所以哀矜女弱，蠲明法制之本分也。 臣以為在室之女，從父母之誅； 既醮之婦，從夫家之罰。 宜改舊科，以為永制。 」於是有詔改定律令。
Under Sima Shi's regency, Wei law still extended capital guilt for great treason to married-out daughters. When Guanqiu Jian fell, his daughter-in-law Lady Xun faced death as kin; her kinsman Xun Yi, tied by marriage to Sima Shi, appealed through the Wei throne to spare her. The court allowed the couple to divorce. Lady Xun's daughter Zhi, wife of Yingchuan governor Liu Ziyuan, was likewise condemned; pregnancy held her in jail. Lady Xun threw herself on He Zeng's mercy, offering to become a state bondmaid to buy her daughter's life. He Zeng took pity and had chief clerk Cheng Xian argue: "The minister of justice frames the code in three grades; the lords of Fu balanced severity and leniency in punishment. Later ages shifted constantly: Qin piled on capital crimes, Han revised them again. Wei still bore Qin and Han's harsh habits; executing married daughters was meant to wipe out villainous lines. Yet law should seek the middle path, and penalties must not overshoot their mark. Women live by the Three Obediences and cannot act alone; once married out, they wear lighter mourning for birth parents to show they belong to another house—not the same as a girl still at home. Yet the code still punished married daughters for their parents' crimes. When a husband's kin were wiped out, wives died for a name no longer theirs. One body thus bore double execution from two families. A married woman belongs to her husband's clan. If she bears sons, she is another line's mother—precisely what villains overlook. Slaughtering innocents weighs cruelly on the victim yet does little to stop rebellion, and it breaks filial hearts. Men escape one clan's guilt while women die twice over—hardly compassion for the weak or a clear boundary in the law. Girls still at home may share their parents' sentence. Wives who have drunk the nuptial cup should answer only to the husband's kin. The old rule should be rewritten as permanent law. An edict followed, ordering a full revision of the code.
24
文帝為晉王，患前代律令本注煩雜，陳群、劉邵雖經改革，而科網本密，又叔孫、郭、馬、杜諸儒章句，但取鄭氏，又為偏黨，未可承用。 於是令賈充定法律，令與太傅鄭沖、司徒荀顗、中書監荀勖、中軍將軍羊祜、中護軍王業、廷尉杜友、守河南尹杜預、散騎侍郎裴楷、潁川太守周雄、齊相郭頎、騎都尉成公綏、尚書郎柳軌及吏部令史榮邵等十四人典其事，就漢九章增十一篇，仍其族類，正其體號，改舊律為《刑名》、《法例》，辨《囚律》為《告劾》、《系訊》、《斷獄》，分《盜律》為《請賕》、《詐偽》、《水火》、《毀亡》，因事類為《衛宮》、《違制》，撰《周官》為《諸侯律》，合二十篇，六百二十條，二萬七千六百五十七言。 蠲其苛穢，存其清約，事從中典，歸於益時。 其餘未宜除者，若軍事、田農、酤酒，未得皆從人心，權設其法，太平當除，故不入律，悉以為令。 施行制度，以此設教，違令有罪則入律。 其常事品式章程，各還其府，為故事。 減梟斬族誅從坐之條，除謀反適養母出女嫁皆不復還坐父母棄市，省禁固相告之條，去捕亡、亡沒為官奴婢之制。 輕過誤老少女人當罰金杖罰者，皆令半之。 重奸伯叔母之令，棄市。 淫寡女，三歲刑。 崇嫁娶之要，一以下娉為正，不理私約。 峻禮教之防，准五服以制罪也。 凡律令合二千九百二十六條，十二萬六千三百言，六十卷，故事三十卷。 泰始三年，事畢，表上。 武帝詔曰：「昔蕭何以定律令受封，叔孫通制儀為奉常，賜金五百斤，弟子百人皆為郎。 夫立功立事，古今之所重，宜加祿賞，其詳考差敘。 輒如詔簡異弟子百人，隨才品用，賞帛萬餘匹。 」武帝親自臨講，使裴楷執讀。 四年正月，大赦天下，乃班新律。
As Jin Prince Sima Yan found earlier codes and glosses tangled; though Chen Qun and Liu Shao had revised them, the mesh stayed tight, and reliance on Zheng Xuan alone skewed interpretation.' He charged Jia Chong, Zheng Chong, Xun Yi, Xun Xu, Yang Hu, Wang Ye, Du You, Du Yu, Pei Kai, Zhou Xiong, Guo Yi, Cheng Gongzui, Liu Gui, and Rong Shao—fourteen officials—to recodify Han's nine chapters into twenty books and 620 clauses (27,657 graphs), splitting old chapters into Names of Punishments and Legal Examples, adding new trial and arrest titles, subdividing robbery and fraud law, adding palace guard and breach-of-regulations chapters, and folding Zhou offices material into a feudal lords statute. They stripped cruelty and clutter, kept essentials, aimed at the mean, and tuned the code to the age. Matters like military law, land tax, and liquor sales stayed outside the code as provisional orders until peace allowed repeal. Breaches of administrative orders became penal only when written into the main code. Day-to-day bureaucratic rules went back to their ministries as precedent compilations. They softened kin liability for treason, spared married daughters and certain in-laws from market execution, dropped mutual-denunciation house arrest, and repealed fugitive enslavement rules. Fines and beatings for minors, elders, women, and minor faults were halved. Incest with a paternal uncle's wife brought public execution. Fornication with widows earned three years' labor. Marriage validity rested on formal betrothal, not private side deals. They tightened ritual fences, tying sentence severity to mourning grades. The finished corpus ran to 2,926 articles, 126,300 characters, sixty rolls of code, and thirty of precedent. In 267 the work ended and was presented to the throne. Emperor Wu decreed that Xiao He had won a fief for codifying law, and Shusun Tong had become grand master of ceremonies with five hundred pounds of gold and a hundred disciples raised to courtiers. Service to the state deserved reward—the compilers were to be ranked and paid accordingly. A hundred talented assistants were to be chosen for office and granted more than ten thousand bolts of silk. The emperor himself presided while Pei Kai read the text aloud. In the first month of 268 he declared a general amnesty and published the new code.
25
其後，明法掾張裴又注律，表上之，其要曰：
Later, legal clerk Zhang Fei added a commentary and presented its gist:
26
律始於《刑名》者，所以定罪制也； 終於《諸侯》者，所以畢其政也。 王政布于上，諸侯奉于下，禮樂撫於中，故有三才之義焉，其相須而成，若一體焉。
The code opens with "Names of Punishments" to define offenses and the system; It closes with "Feudal Lords" to round out public governance. Throne, vassals, and rites form a triad like heaven, earth, and man—each limb needing the others.
27
《刑名》所以經略罪法之輕重，正加減之等差，明發眾篇之多義，補其章條之不足，較舉上下綱領。 其犯盜賊、詐偽、請賕者，則求罪於此，作役、水火、畜養、守備之細事，皆求之作本名。 告訊為之心舌，捕系為之手足，斷獄為之定罪，名例齊其制。 自始及終，往而不窮，變動無常，周流四極，上下無方，不離於法律之中也。
"Names of Punishments" sets the scale of penalties, grades commutations, explains cross-references, fills gaps, and states the code's spine. Robbery, fraud, and bribery are judged here; corvée, fire, flood, herd, and guard offenses keep their chapter titles. Denunciation and trial are the code's voice and mind, arrest and jail its hands and feet, judgment its verdict, and the general part ties the system together. It runs start to finish without exhausting its cases, shifts flexibly, reaches every corner, yet never steps outside the written law.
28
其知而犯之謂之故，意以為然謂之失，違忠欺上謂之謾，背信藏巧謂之詐，虧禮廢節謂之不敬，兩訟相趣謂之鬥，兩和相害謂之戲，無變斬擊謂之賊，不意誤犯謂之過失，逆節絕理謂之不道，陵上僭貴謂之惡逆，將害未發謂之戕，唱首先言謂之造意，二人對議謂之謀，制眾建計謂之率，不和謂之強，攻惡謂之略，三人謂之群，取非其物謂之盜，貨財之利謂之贓：凡二十者，律義之較名也。
Knowing wrong and doing it is "intent"; misjudging motive is "mistake"; deceiving a lord is "cheating"; hiding guile is "fraud"; breaching ritual is "disrespect"; mutual lawsuits are "brawl"; agreed dueling harm is "sport"; sudden killing is "robbery"; unintended harm is "error"; defying cosmic order is "immoral"; usurping rank is "vicious treason"; intent short of act is "malice"; instigating is "origination"; pair plotting is "conspiracy"; ringleading is "orchestration"; coercion is "force"; predation is "raid"; three or more is "gang"; wrongful taking is "theft"; illicit gain is "graft"—twenty keywords that map the code.
29
夫律者，當慎其變，審其理。 若不承用詔書，無故失之刑，當從贖。 謀反之同伍，實不知情，當從刑。 此故失之變也。 卑與尊鬥，皆為賊。 鬥之加兵刃水火中，不得為戲，戲之重也。 向人室廬道徑射，不得為過，失之禁也。 都城人眾中走馬殺人，當為賊，賊之似也。 過失似賊，戲似鬥，鬥而殺傷傍人，又似誤，盜傷縛守似強盜，呵人取財似受賕，囚辭所連似告劾，諸勿聽理似故縱，持質似恐猲。 如此之比，皆為無常之格也。
Statutes demand care with variation and clear grasp of principle. Neglecting an imperial rescript without malice is redeemable. Neighbors of traitors who were truly ignorant should take the lighter derivative sentence, not the full traitor's penalty. Such are the borderline cases of intent versus error. A commoner who strikes a superior counts as banditry. Once blades, fire, or water enter a fight, it is no longer mere "sport" but a graver crime. Shooting toward someone's home or path is not dismissed as accident—it violates the ban on reckless harm. Galloping through a thronged capital street and killing counts as banditry by analogy. Accident can look like robbery, horseplay like brawl, brawl like mishap, theft-injury like armed robbery, shakedown like bribery, jailhouse tales like denunciation, ignored pleas like connivance, seizure like extortion. These analogies form a grid of shifting standards.
30
五刑不簡，正於五罰，五罰不服，正於五過，意善功惡，以金贖之。 故律制，生罪不過十四等，死刑不過三，徒加不過六，囚加不過五，累作不過十一歲，累笞不過千二百，刑等不過一歲，金等不過四兩。 月贖不計日，日作不拘月，歲數不疑閏。 不以加至死，並死不復加。 不可累者，故有並數； 不可並數，乃累其加。 以加論者，但得其加； 與加同者，連得其本。 不在次者，不以通論。 以人得罪與人同，以法得罪與法同。 侵生害死，不可齊其防； 親疏公私，不可常其教。 禮樂崇於上，故降其刑； 刑法閑于下，故全其法。 是故尊卑敘，仁義明，九族親，王道平也。
When the five punishments misfire, use fines; when fines fail, use the five pardons—good intent but bad outcome may be bought off with copper. The code caps living offenses at fourteen grades, death at three, labor additions at six, jail extensions at five, total labor at eleven years, total blows at 1,200, single-grade jumps at one year, and fines at four taels. Redemption by month ignores odd days; daily labor ignores calendar months; yearly sentences ignore leap insertion. Aggravation must not stack to unintended death; where death already applies, nothing stacks beyond. Incommensurable penalties use combined reckoning;' where combination fails, successive aggravations apply. In aggravated sentencing, apply only the top increment;' when increments match, trace back to the base crime. Offenses outside the listed ladder are not inferred by loose analogy. Personal crimes follow personal rules; statutory crimes follow the statute. Harm to the living and the dead cannot share one rule;' Kin, strangers, public, and private wrongs cannot use one fixed lesson. Where rites rank high, penalties drop;' where law runs the streets, the full statute applies. Thus rank orders itself, humanity and duty shine, nine degrees of kin draw close, and the royal path runs level.
31
律有事狀相似而罪名相涉者，若加威勢下手取財為強盜，不自知亡為縛守，將中有惡言為恐猲，不以罪名呵為呵人，以罪名呵為受賕，劫召其財為持質。 此六者，以威勢得財而名殊者也。 即不求自與為受求，所監求而後取為盜贓，輸入呵受為留難，斂人財物積藏於官為擅賦，加歐擊之為戮辱。 諸如此類，皆為以威勢得財而罪相似者也。
The code lists six ways force yields property yet bears different names: armed robbery, fugitive taken as guard, ringleader's threats as extortion, naked demand as "hectoring," named offense demand as bribery, seizure-for-ransom as hostage-taking. Six labels for coercion that differ in nuance. Gifts unasked are "solicited bribes," takings after supervised demand are "theft by office," scripted harassment is "obstruction," hoarded public levies are "illegal tax," and added beating is "humiliating assault."' All are forceful takings that look alike yet fall under different crimes.
32
夫刑者，司理之官； 理者，求情之機，情者，心神之使。 心感則情動於中，而形於言？ 暢于四支，發於事業。 是故奸人心愧而面赤，內怖而色奪。 論罪者務本其心，審其情，精其事，近取諸身，遠取諸物，然後乃可以正刑。 仰手似乞，俯手似奪，捧手似謝，擬手似訴，拱臂似自首，攘臂似格鬥，矜莊似威，怡悅似福，喜怒憂歡，貌在聲色。 奸真猛弱，候在視息。 出口有言當為告，下手有禁當為賊，喜子殺怒子當為戲，怒子殺喜子當為賊。 諸如此類，自非至精不能極其理也。
Law is the office of reason;' reason is the lever on motive; motive is the mind's envoy. When the heart stirs, emotion moves inside and shows in words—does it not? It reaches the four limbs and spills into action. Hence the guilty blush and blanch by turns. Judges must trace mind and motive, weigh facts, read body language and material clues—only then may sentence be just. Uplifted palms plead, lowered hands grab, cupped hands thank, pointed fingers accuse, folded arms confess, flung arms fight, stern face feigns dignity, soft face feigns kindness—passion plays on voice and skin. Truth of malice, force of violence, hide in eyes and breath. Spoken threat is denunciation; forbidden blow is robbery; killing a furious child in jest is "sport"; killing a playful child in rage is robbery. Only the subtlest mind can exhaust such distinctions.
33
律之名例，非正文而分明也。 若八十，非殺傷人，他皆勿論，即誣告謀反者反坐。 十歲，不得告言人； 即奴婢捍主，主得謁殺之。 賊燔人廬舍積聚，盜贓五匹以上，棄市； 即燔官府積聚盜，亦當與同。 歐人教令者與同罪，即令人歐其父母，不可與行者同得重也。 若得遺物強取強乞之類，無還贓法隨例畀之文。 法律中諸不敬，違儀失式，及犯罪為公為私，贓入身不入身，皆隨事輕重取法，以例求其名也。
The code's "definitions and examples" are not operative articles yet make the rules transparent. At eighty one was not prosecuted except for homicide or injury, while false accusers of treason suffered the same penalty they sought. Children under ten could not lodge accusations. A bondservant who struck the master could be killed on the master's petition. Arson of private dwellings with theft over five bolts of goods brought execution in the market; the same rule applied to torching government granaries and theft. Instigating a beating shared the beater's sentence, but ordering a son to beat his parents could not be equated with ordinary abetting. Forced seizure of lost property lacked a restitution rule, so courts followed analogous clauses. Disrespect, ritual lapses, and public versus private guilt, with or without personal enrichment, were graded by circumstance and matched to named offenses.
34
夫理者，精玄之妙，不可以一方行也； 律者，幽理之奧，不可以一體守也。 或計過以配罪，或化略以循常，或隨事以盡情，或趣舍以從時，或推重以立防，或引輕而就下。 公私廢避之宜，除削重輕之變，皆所以臨時觀釁，使用法執詮者幽於未制之中，采其根牙之微，致之於機格之上，稱輕重於豪銖，考輩類于參伍，然後乃可以理直刑正。
Principle is too subtle for a single formula; the code's inner logic cannot be grasped from one rigid template. Judges might weigh fault, simplify routine cases, follow facts to plumb motive, bend to the times, set harsh precedents as warnings, or lean lenient. Rules on conflict of interest and sentence adjustment let judges read each case's grain, trace roots beneath unwritten gaps, slot facts into statutory frames, balance weight to the hair, and cross-check analogies—only then was justice straight.
35
夫奉聖典者若操刀執繩，刀妄加則傷物，繩妄彈則侵直。 梟首者惡之長，斬刑者罪之大，棄市者死之下，髡作者刑之威，贖罰者誤之誡。 王者立此五刑，所以寶君子而逼小人，故為敕慎之經，皆擬《周易》有變通之體焉。 欲令提綱而大道清，舉略而王法齊，其旨遠，其辭文，其言曲而中，其事肆而隱。 通天下之志唯忠也，斷天下之疑唯文也，切天下之情唯遠也，彌天下之務唯大也，變無常體唯理也，非天下之賢聖，孰能與於斯！
Applying the classics is like wielding blade and plumb: careless cuts harm the innocent, careless lines warp what is straight. Head-display marked supreme villainy, waist-cutting the gravest crime, market execution the least of capital penalties, shaved labor the fearsome middle, fines the caution for mistakes. The five punishments honored the good and cowed the wicked, framed as carefully as the Zhou "Changes" with its language of adaptation. They meant to lift the main rope so the Way cleared, sketch essentials so royal law aligned—aiming high, wording elegantly, speaking obliquely yet truly, covering much while hinting more. Loyalty reads every heart, culture settles every doubt, distance measures every passion, greatness handles every task, principle shifts without fixed mask—and none but sages could master it.
36
夫刑而上者謂之道，刑而下者謂之器，化而裁之謂之格。 刑殺者是冬震曜之象，髡罪者似秋雕落之變，贖失者是春陽悔吝之疵之。 五刑成章，輒相依准，法律之義焉。
Philosophy sits above the statute blade; procedure is the implement below; wise judges trim each case to fit the living norm. Death sentences are winter's thunderbolt; mutilation is autumn's stripping leaves; redeemable fault is spring warmth marred by regret. Once the five punishments formed a coherent ladder, each grade checked the next—that was the spirit of the code.
37
是時侍中盧珽、中書侍郎張華又表：「抄《新律》諸死罪條目，懸之亭傳，以示兆庶。 」有詔從之。
Attendant Lu Yan and Zhang Hua asked that every capital clause of the New Code be posted at relay stations for the people to read. The throne agreed.
38
及劉頌為廷尉，頻表宜復肉刑，不見省，又上言曰：
Liu Song, as commandant of justice, urged corporal punishment again and again without reply, then wrote further:
39
臣昔上行肉刑，從來積年，遂寢不論。 臣竊以為議者拘孝文之小仁，而輕違聖王之典刑，未詳之甚，莫過於此。
I have long urged restoring mutilating penalties, yet year after year the matter has slept. Critics cling to Emperor Wen's mildness and ignore the sages' code—nothing could be more shortsighted.
40
今死刑重，故非命者眾； 生刑輕，故罪不禁奸。 所以然者，肉刑不用之所致也。 今為徒者，類性元惡不軌之族也，去家懸遠，作役山谷，饑寒切身，志不聊生，雖有廉士介者，苟慮不首死，則皆為盜賊，豈況本性奸凶無賴之徒乎！ 又令徒富者輸財，解日歸家，乃無役之人也。 貧者起為奸盜，又不制之虜也。 不刑，則罪無所禁； 不制，則群惡橫肆。 為法若此，近不盡善也。 是以徒亡日屬，賊盜日煩，亡之數者至有十數，得輒加刑，日益一歲，此為終身之徒也。 自顧反善無期，而災困逼身，其志亡思盜，勢不得息，事使之然也。
Capital crimes are so harsh that many die untimely; lesser penalties are so light that crime goes unchecked. This imbalance comes from abandoning corporal punishment. Today's convicts are mostly hardened villains, torn from home and worked in the hills until cold and hunger break them; even an honest man, seeing only death ahead, turns thief, let alone born ruffians. The rich buy off their term and walk free—never having labored at all. The poor graduate to banditry and slip beyond control. Without real punishment crime knows no bar; without control wickedness spreads unchecked. Such a system falls far short of the good. Escapes chain daily, theft prospers; some run ten times or more, each capture adding a year until a man is a convict for life. Seeing no path to reform, crushed by misery, they can think only of theft—policy drives them to it.
41
古者用刑以止刑，今反於此。 諸重犯亡者，發過三寸輒重髡之，此以刑生刑； 加作一歲，此以徒生徒也。 亡者積多，系囚猥畜。 議者曰囚不可不赦，復從而赦之，此為刑不制罪，法不勝奸。 下知法之不勝，相聚而謀為不軌，月異而歲不同。 故自頃年以來，奸惡陵暴，所在充斥。 議者不深思此故，而曰肉刑於名忤聽，忤聽孰與賊盜不禁？
Ancient law ended crime; ours breeds it. Serious fugitives, once hair tops three inches, are shaved again—punishment breeding punishment; each capture adds a year—labor breeding labor. Fugitives multiply and jails swell. Reformers cry "amnesty" until pardons outrun crime—law no longer masters the wicked. Criminals learn the code cannot catch them and plot ever bolder outrages month by month. Hence in recent years outrage has flooded every district. They fret that corporal punishment "sounds cruel" yet ignore unchecked banditry—which offends the ear more?
42
聖王之制肉刑，遠有深理，其事可得而言，非徒懲其畏剝割之痛而不為也，乃去其為惡之具，使夫奸人無用復肆其志，止奸絕本，理之盡也。 亡者刖足，無所用復亡。 盜者截手，無所用復盜。 淫者割其勢，理亦如之。 除惡塞源，莫善於此，非徒然也。 此等已刑之後，便各歸家，父母妻子，共相養恤，不流離于塗路。 有今之困，創愈可役，上准古制，隨宜業作，雖已刑殘，不為虛棄，而所患都塞，又生育繁阜之道自若也。
Sage kings mutilated not only to terrify but to remove the very organs of crime so villains could not reoffend—that was rooting out evil. A footless fugitive cannot run again. A handless thief cannot steal again. Rapists were castrated on the same logic. Nothing better purges the source of evil. After mutilation they could go home to family support instead of rotting on the road. Once healed, the mutilated could do light corvée suited to their maiming—useful to the state, not wasted, while crime dried up and population grew as before.
43
今宜取死刑之限輕，及三犯逃亡淫盜，悉以肉刑代之。 其三歲刑以下，已自杖罰遣，又宜制其罰數，使有常限，不得減此。 其有宜重者，又任之官長。 應四五歲刑者，皆髡笞，笞至一百，稍行，使各有差，悉不復居作。 然後刑不復生刑，徒不復生徒，而殘體為戳，終身作誡。 人見其痛，畏而不犯，必數倍於今。 且為惡者隨發被刑，去其為惡之具，此為諸已刑者皆良士也，豈與全其為奸之手足，而蹴居必死之窮地同哉！ 而猶曰肉刑不可用，臣竊以為不識務之甚也。
Capital cases on the lighter side, plus thrice-fled convicts, rapists, and robbers, should be commuted to corporal punishment. Sentences under three years, already dismissed after caning, should have fixed stroke counts that cannot be cut further. Heavier cases stayed with the presiding magistrate. Four- or five-year terms became shaving plus up to one hundred strokes of bamboo, staggered by degree, without long convict labor. Then punishment would no longer spiral, nor labor endlessly compound, while visible maiming warned for life. Seeing the pain, men would fear to offend—many times more effective than today. The punished villain loses the means to sin and becomes a harmless neighbor—far better than leaving his wicked limbs intact only to march him to certain death. To say mutilation is unusable is to misunderstand the problem utterly.
44
臣昔常侍左右，數聞明詔，謂肉刑宜用，事便於政。 願陛下信獨見之斷，使夫能者得奉聖慮，行之於今。 比填溝壑，冀見太平。 《周禮》三赦三宥，施於老幼悼耄，黔黎不屬逮者，此非為惡之所出，故刑法逆舍而宥之。 至於自非此族，犯罪則必刑而無赦，此政之理也。 暨至後世，以時嶮多難，因赦解結，權以行之，又不以寬罪人也。 至今恆以罪積獄繁，赦以散之，是以赦愈數而獄愈塞，如此不已，將至不勝。 原其所由，內刑不用之故也。 今行肉刑，非徒不積，且為惡無具則奸息。 去此二端，獄不得繁，故無取於數赦，於政體勝矣。
I often heard Your Majesty say corporal punishment served good government. Trust your own judgment and let able ministers enact what the throne has long favored. I would gladly die in a ditch could I see the realm at peace. The Zhou three pardons covered infants, elders, and accidental offenders—not born criminals—so the code waived them. Anyone outside that class who broke the law was punished without pardon—that was just rule. Later dynasties, beset by trouble, used amnesty tactically, not to cheapen guilt. Today amnesties clear crowded jails, yet each pardon refills them—if this continues, the system will collapse. The root cause is the refusal to use corporal punishment. Corporal law would thin the jails and strip villains of means to reoffend. Cut both roots and jails stay clear—no need of endless pardons; that is sound government.
45
疏上，又不見省。
His memorial went unanswered again.
46
至惠帝之世，政出群下，每有疑獄，各立私情，刑法不定，獄訟繁滋。 尚書裴頠表陳之曰：
Under Emperor Hui, ministers ran the court; each doubtful case followed private bias, the code wavered, and litigation exploded. Minister Pei Wei wrote:
47
夫天下之事多塗，非一司之所管； 中才之情易擾，賴恆制而後定。 先王知其所以然也，是以辨方分職，為之准局。 准局既立，各掌其務，刑賞相稱，輕重無二，故下聽有常，群吏安業也。 舊宮掖陵廟有水火毀傷之變，然後尚書乃躬自奔赴，其非此也，皆止于郎令史而已。 刑罰所加，各有常刑。
The realm's business has many channels—no single bureau can hold it all; average minds waver until fixed rules steady them. The ancients knew this, so they carved duties into clear jurisdictions. With clear portfolios, reward and penalty align, severity stays even, clerks know their lane, and the machine runs. Only fire or flood at palace or temple drew the minister in person; lesser calls stopped at section clerks. Each offense carried its set penalty.
48
去元康四年，大風之後，廟闕屋瓦有數枚傾落，免太常荀寓。 于時以嚴詔所譴，莫敢據正。 然內外之意，僉謂事輕責重，有違于常。 會五年二月有大風，主者懲懼前事。 臣新拜尚書始三日，本曹尚書有疾，權令兼出，按行蘭台。 主者乃瞻望阿棟之間，求索瓦之不正者，得棟上瓦小邪十五處。 或是始瓦時邪，蓋不足言，風起倉卒，台官更往，太常按行，不及得周，文書未至之頃，便競相禁止。 臣以權兼暫出，出還便罷，不復得窮其事。 而本曹據執，卻問無已。 臣時具加解遣，而主者畏咎，不從臣言，禁止太常，復興刑獄。
In 294, after a gale dislodged a few temple roof tiles, Grand Master Xun Yu was dismissed. Under the emperor's harsh tone no one dared speak straight law. Yet everyone felt the fault slight and punishment harsh—against norm. When another gale struck in the fifth year's second month, officials trembled at the precedent. I had been minister of reading three days when my chief fell ill and I was sent to inspect the Orchid Terrace. Inspectors scanned the rafters, found fifteen slightly crooked tiles— likely set crooked at construction, hardly a crime; wind rose, boards rushed out, the grand master could not finish his round before paperwork flew and everyone froze in panic. I was acting chief, returned when relieved, and could not pursue the matter further. Yet my office kept the docket open and nagged endlessly. I explained the nonsense away, but the clerks, fearing blame, ignored me, barred the grand master, and reopened a criminal case.
49
昔漢氏有盜廟玉環者，文帝欲族誅，釋之但處以死刑，曰：「若侵長陵一抔土，何以復加？ 」文帝從之。 大晉垂制，深惟經遠，山陵不封，園邑不飾，墓而不墳，同乎山壤，是以丘阪存其陳草，使齊乎中原矣。 雖陵兆尊嚴，唯毀發然後族之，此古典也。 若登踐犯損，失盡敬之道，事止刑罪可也。
When a man stole a temple jade ring, Emperor Wen wanted kin execution; Zhang Shizhi gave death alone, asking, "Had he stolen a cup of earth from the imperial mound, what worse could you add?" The emperor yielded. Our Jin shrines lie low—no sealed tumuli, no park walls, tombs flush with the soil like open hills—so a snapped twig should weigh no more than damage to wild grass. Kin execution should follow only true desecration—that was classical rule. Trampling carelessly might merit only ordinary sentence.
50
去八年，奴聽教加誣周龍燒草，廷尉遂奏族龍，一門八口並命。 會龍獄翻，然後得免。 考之情理，准之前訓，所處實重。 今年八月，陵上荊一枝圍七寸二分者被斫，司徒太常，奔走道路，雖知事小，而案劾難測，搔擾驅馳，各競免負，於今太常禁止未解。 近日太祝署失火，燒屋三間半。 署在廟北，隔道在重牆之內，又即已滅，頻為詔旨所問。 主者以詔旨使問頻繁，便責尚書不即案行，輒禁止，尚書免，皆在法外。
Eight years back a slave, coached, swore Zhou Long burned brush; the commandant sought clan execution—eight lives. A retrial spared them. Measured against precedent, that prosecution was cruelly heavy. This August someone lopped a seven-inch bramble on the imperial mound; high ministers stampeded, knowing the act trivial yet fearing unpredictable charges, each dodging blame—the grand master of ceremonies remains suspended still. Lately the invocators' office burned three and a half rooms. It stood north of the temple, behind double walls across a lane, and the fire was out—yet edicts kept demanding answers. Clerks, badgered by repeated imperial queries, faulted the minister of reading for not rushing to inspect, barred him, and secured his dismissal—none of it statutory.
51
刑書之文有限，而舛違之故無方，故有臨時議處之制，誠不能皆得循常也。 至於此等，皆為過當，每相逼迫，不得以理，上替聖朝畫一之德，下損崇禮大臣之望。 臣愚以為犯陵上草木，不應乃用同產異刑之制。 按行奏劾，應有定準，相承務重，體例遂虧。 或因余事，得容淺深。
Written law is finite but human mischief is infinite, so ad hoc rulings exist—yet not every case can fit a template. Such overreach bullies the parties, betrays reason, tarnishes the throne's uniform justice, and wounds great ministers who stand for decorum. Damaging tomb vegetation should not trigger the same kin-guilt statutes as attacking the shrine itself. Inspection and indictment need clear standards; competing to be harsh erodes the whole system. Other factors may still shade severity.
52
頠雖有此表，曲議猶不止。 時劉頌為三公尚書，又上疏曰：
Even after Pei Wei's paper, wrangling continued. Liu Song, as senior minister of state, memorialized again:
53
自近世以來，法漸多門，令甚不一。 臣今備掌刑斷，職思其憂，謹具啟聞。
In recent times law has sprouted many doors and edicts no longer agree. I now hold judicial office and must voice its perils.
54
臣竊伏惟陛下為政，每盡善，故事求曲當，則例不得直； 盡善，故法不得全。 何則？ 夫法者，固以盡理為法，而上求盡善，則諸下牽文就意，以赴主之所許，是以法不得全。 刑書徵文，徵文必有乖於情聽之斷，而上安于曲當，故執平者因文可引，則生二端。 是法多門，令不一，則吏不知所守，下不知所避。 奸偽者因法之多門，以售其情，所欲淺深，苟斷不一，則居上者難以檢下，於是事同議異，獄犴不平，有傷於法。
Your Majesty always seeks the perfect outcome, so in cases you bend precedent to fit— yet chasing perfect justice shatters consistent law. Why? Law should exhaust rational rules, but if the throne demands perfect outcomes, clerks twist clauses to please you—so the code splinters. Literal reading clashes with equitable sense; if the ruler settles for "close enough," judges split hairs and fork outcomes. Many doors to law leave clerks unsure what to enforce and people unsure what to fear. Knaves shop forums until they find a favorable clause; inconsistent rulings let crime hide from superiors, identical facts draw opposite verdicts, and justice itself is wounded.
55
古人有言：「人主詳，其政荒； 人主期，其事理。 」詳匪他，盡善則法傷，故其政荒也。 期者輕重之當，雖不厭情，苟入于文，則循而行之，故其事理也。 夫善用法者，忍違情不厭聽之斷，輕重雖不允人心，經於凡覽，若不可行，法乃得直。 又君臣之分，各有所司。 法欲必奉，故令主者守文； 理有窮塞，故使大臣釋滯； 事有時宜，故人主權斷。 主者守文，若釋之執犯蹕之平也； 大臣釋滯，若公孫弘斷郭解之獄也； 人主權斷，若漢祖戮丁公之為也。 天下萬事，自非斯格重為，故不近似此類，不得出以意妄議，其餘皆以律令從事。 然後法信於下，人聽不惑，吏不容奸，可以言政。 人主軌斯格以責群下，大臣小吏各守其局，則法一矣。
The classics warn: a fussy sovereign wastes the realm; a ruler who sets clear rules brings order. Micromanagement is not benign—it breaks law and ruins government. Deadlines mean steady scales of severity; even when equity grumbles, if it is written, apply it—and affairs stay ordered. Good jurists accept unpopular verdicts; even when the crowd hates the weight of sentence, if the code demands it, enforcing the text is what makes law straight. Ruler and minister each have a sphere. Statutes must be absolute—clerks hold the written rule; principle can deadlock—great ministers untie it; policy shifts with the hour—the sovereign decides exceptions. Clerks sticking to text are Zhang Shizhi fining a mere boundary breach. ministers breaking deadlock are Gongsun Hong closing Guo Jie's case; royal discretion is Gaozu executing Ding Gong for treason to a new lord. Save for rare cases of state magnitude, nothing should be argued outside the code; everything else follows statute and edict. Then law wins trust, the people hear one tune, clerks cannot hide graft, and one may call it rule. The ruler enforces this division so ministers and clerks stay in lane—then law is one.
56
古人有言：「善為政者，看人設教。 」看人設教，制法之謂也。 又曰：「隨時之宜」，當務之謂也。 然則看人隨時，在大量也，而制其法。 法軌既定則行之，行之信如四時，執之堅如金石，群吏豈得在成制之內，復稱隨時之宜，傍引看人設教，以亂政典哉！ 何則？ 始制之初，固已看人而隨時矣。 今若設法未盡當，則宜改之。 若謂已善，不得盡以為制，而使奉用之司公得出入以差輕重也。 夫人君所與天下共者，法也。 已令四海，不可以不信以為教，方求天下之不慢，不可繩以不信之法。 且先識有言，人至遇而不可欺也。 不謂平時背法意斷，不勝百姓願也。
The sages said good rule teaches to the people you have; tailoring law to the people is what codification means. They also said meet the times—that is serving the urgent need. People and seasons both feed the grand design that shapes the code. Once promulgated, law must run like seasons and stand like bronze—clerks may not reopen "flexible" pleas to wreck the statute book. Why? The founders already baked people and times into the text. If clauses misfire, amend them openly. If the code is sound, clerks may not privately bend weight to taste. Law is the covenant between throne and realm. Having commanded the world, the throne cannot teach distrust; demanding diligence while waving inconsistent statutes is impossible. The ancients said the people may be met but not fooled. It does not license peacetime caprice against the code to please the mob.
57
上古議事以制，不為刑辟。 夏殷及周，書法象魏。 三代之君齊聖，然咸棄曲當之妙鑒，而任徵文之直准，非聖有殊，所遇異也。 今論時敦樸，不及中古，而執平者欲適情之所安，自托於議事以制。 臣竊以為聽言則美，論理則違。 然天下至大，事務眾雜，時有不得悉循文如令。 故臣謂宜立格為限，使主者守文，死生以之，不敢錯思于成制之外，以差輕重，則法恆全。 事無正據，名例不及，大臣論當，以釋不滯，則事無閡。 至如非常之斷，出法賞罰，若漢祖戮楚臣之私己，封趙氏之無功，唯人主專之，非奉職之臣所得擬議。 然後情求傍請之跡絕，似是而非之奏塞，此蓋齊法之大准也。 主者小吏，處事無常。 何則？ 無情則法徒克，有情則撓法。 積克似無私，然乃所以得其私，又恆所岨以衛其身。 斷當恆克，世謂盡公，時一曲法，乃所不疑。 故人君不善倚深似公之斷，而責守文如令之奏，然後得為有檢，此又平法之一端也。
Highest antiquity decided cases without written penalties. Xia, Shang, and Zhou published statutes on the gate-boards. Those sage kings were equally holy, yet they dropped ad hoc cleverness for written rules—not different wisdom, different ages. Today is rougher than middle antiquity, yet judges still invoke "rule by circumstance" to chase comfort. It sounds virtuous but breaks jurisprudence. The realm is vast and business tangled—some cases will not fit the letter. Set bright limits: clerks apply the written rule to life-and-death cases without improvising shades—then the code stays intact. Where facts lack a hook and the general part is silent, ministers settle the logjam. Royal rewards and killings outside the statute—like Gaozu killing Ding Gong or enfeoffing favorites—belong to the sovereign alone, not to clerks. Then backdoor pleas die and sophistries end—that is even justice. Front-line clerks shift rulings capriciously. Why? Cold logic makes cruel sentences; private sympathy bends the code. Harshness masquerades as impartiality yet hides private safety; routine severity passes for integrity while occasional leniency draws no blame. Rulers should distrust "fair" cruelty and demand letter-perfect filings—another pillar of balanced law.
58
夫出法權制，指施一事，厭情合聽，可適耳目，誠有臨時當意之快，勝於徵文不允人心也。 然起為經制，經年施用，恆得一而失十。 故小有所得者，必大有所失； 近有所漏者，必遠有所苞。 故諳事識體者，善權輕重，不以小害大，不以近妨遠。 忍曲當之近適，以全簡直之大准。 不牽於凡聽之所安，必守徵文以正例。 每臨其事，恆禦此心以決斷，此又法之大概也。
Ad hoc decrees please the crowd and fix one case faster than rigid text. Elevated to standing rule, they win once and lose ten times over. Small gains bring large losses; plugging a near hole opens a distant breach. Seasoned statesmen weigh whole cloth, never trading a big principle for a small fix. They swallow minor inequity to keep the main line straight. They refuse mob comfort and cling to written precedent. Every case should be met with that discipline—that is the spirit of the code.
59
又律法斷罪，皆當以法律令正文，若無正文，依附名例斷之，其正文名例所不及，皆勿論。 法吏以上，所執不同，得為異議。 如律之文，守法之官，唯當奉用律令。 至於法律之內，所見不同，乃得為異議也。 今限法曹郎令史，意有不同為駁，唯得論釋法律，以正所斷，不得援求諸外，論隨時之宜，以明法官守局之分。
Sentences must cite the operative clause; if none fits, use the general part; if still silent, dismiss the charge. Officials above law-clerk rank may file dissenting readings. Trial judges must apply the written word. Disagreement on intra-code interpretation is allowed. Let code-section clerks rebut only on statutory gloss, never on policy whims—clarifying each judge's lane.
60
詔下其事。 侍中、太宰、汝南王亮奏以為：「夫禮以訓世，而法以整俗，理化之本，事實由之。 若斷不斷，常輕重隨意，則王憲不一，人無所錯矣。 故觀人設教，在上之舉； 守文直法，臣吏之節也。 臣以去太康八年，隨事異議。 周懸象魏之書，漢詠畫一之法，誠以法與時共，義不可二。 今法素定，而法為議，則有所開長，以為宜如頌所啟，為永久之制。 」於是門下屬三公曰：「昔先王議事以制，自中古以來，執法斷事，既以立法，誠不宜復求法外小善也。 若常以善奪法，則人逐善而不忌法，其害甚於無法也。 案啟事，欲令法令斷一，事無二門，郎令史已下，應復出法駁案，隨事以聞也。」
The throne ordered the matter implemented. Prince Sima Liang wrote: ritual teaches the world, law aligns custom—both ground good order. If courts waver, the constitution splinters and the people lose footing. Tailoring teaching is the ruler's prerogative; holding the written line is the minister's duty. Since Taikang 8 (287) each case has spawned new doctrine. Zhou posted statutes, Han praised uniform justice—law must move with the age yet stay single in meaning. The code is settled yet keeps reopening; Liu Song's proposal should become permanent practice. The secretariat ruled: ancient kings judged before codifying; since we have written law, clerks must not chase extra-statutory "kindness." Letting "mercy" overrule statute makes men chase favor and ignore law—worse than anarchy. The petition asks one door for justice: clerks who dissent must cite statute and report up the chain.
61
及于江左，元帝為丞相時，朝廷草創，議斷不循法律，人立異議，高下無狀。 主簿熊遠奏曰：「禮以崇善，法以閑非，故禮有常典，法有常防，人知惡而無邪心。 是以周建象魏之制，漢創畫一之法，故能闡弘大道，以至刑厝。 律令之作，由來尚矣。 經賢智，曆夷險，隨時斟酌，最為周備。 自軍興以來，法度陵替，至於處事不用律令，競作屬命，人立異議，曲適物情，虧傷大例。 府立節度，復不奉用，臨事改制，朝作夕改，至於主者不敢任法，每輒關咨，委之大官，非為政之體。 若本曹處事不合法令，監司當以法彈違，不得動用開塞，以壞成事。 按法蓋粗術，非妙道也，矯割物情，以成法耳。 若每隨物情，輒改法制，此為以情壞法。 法之不一，是謂多門，開人事之路，廣私請之端，非先王立法之本意也。 凡為駁議者，若違律令節度，當合經傳及前比故事，不得任情以破成法。 愚謂宜令錄事更立條制，諸立議者皆當引律令經傳，不得直以情言，無所依准，以虧舊典也。 若開塞隨宜，權道制物，此是人君之所得行，非臣子所宜專用。 主者唯當徵文據法，以事為斷耳。」
South of the river, under Prince Yuan as regent, the court was new; cases ignored the code, every clerk spun his own rule, chaos without shape. Registrar Xiong Yuan wrote: ritual lifts virtue, law fences vice—fixed ritual and fixed law keep hearts straight. Hence Zhou's gate-boards and Han's uniform rule spread the Way until racks stood empty. Codified law is ancient and venerable. Sages refined it through peace and war until it was thorough. Since war began, rules collapsed; offices ignore the code, issue private orders, bend each case to mood, and wound the whole frame. Headquarters issues rules then ignores them, revising dawn to dusk until clerks dare not decide and shove everything upward—bad government. If a ministry breaks statute, censors should strike by law, not stall completed work with red tape. Law is blunt carpentry, not mysticism—it trims facts to fit the rule. Letting every mood rewrite the code is letting passion destroy law. Splintered law becomes many doors—inviting favor and private pleas, not the sages' intent. Dissents must cite classics, commentary, or precedent—never gut-feeling to break settled law. Order record offices: every argument must quote statute or classic, never bare sentiment, lest old canons erode. Flexing policy is the monarch's prerogative, not a clerk's private toy. Judges should cite law and decide facts, nothing more.
62
是時帝以權宜從事，尚未能從。 而河東衛展為晉王大理，考擿故事有不合情者，又上書曰：「今施行詔書，有考子正父死刑，或鞭父母問子所在。 近主者所稱《庚寅詔書》，舉家逃亡家長斬。 若長是逃亡之主，斬之雖重猶可。 設子孫犯事，將考祖父逃亡，逃亡是子孫，而父祖嬰其酷。 傷順破教，如此者眾。 相隱之道離，則君臣之義廢。 君臣之義廢，則犯上之奸生矣。 秦網密文峻，漢興，掃除煩苛，風移俗易，幾于刑厝。 大人革命，不得不蕩其穢匿，通其圮滯。 今詔書宜除者多，有便於當今，著為正條，則法差簡易。 」元帝令曰：「禮樂不興，則刑罰不中，是以明罰敕法，先王所慎。 自元康已來，事故薦臻，法禁滋漫。 大理所上，宜朝堂會議，蠲除詔書不可用者，此孤所虛心者也。」
The regent could not yet adopt the reform. Wei Zhan of Hedong, as the Jin prince's chief judge, found edicts that tortured kin to prove crime and wrote: "Some orders have sons prove fathers capital, or whip parents to find sons. The so-called Gengyin edict beheads the householder when the whole family runs. Executing a fleeing paterfamilias is harsh but fair. But when grandsons sin and torturers grill grandfathers for a flight the young committed, elders die for juniors' acts. That violates natural order and destroys teaching—too often today. Break kin concealment and ruler-minister duty collapses. Without that bond, treason thrives. Qin law was a tight mesh; Han swept it away until racks nearly stood empty. Founding a dynasty must purge old rot and clear blocked justice. Strike bad edicts, codify what still fits—then the code simplifies. Prince Yuan replied: "Without ritual and music, penalties misfire—sage kings weighed every line of law. Since the Yuan-kang years troubles multiplied and statutes swelled. Hold a full court, repeal unworkable edicts—that is my earnest wish.
63
及帝即位，展為廷尉，又上言：「古者肉刑，事經前聖，漢文除之，增加大辟。 今人戶凋荒，百不遺一，而刑法峻重，非句踐養胎之義也。 愚謂宜復古施行，以隆太平之化。 」詔內外通議。 於是驃騎將軍王導、太常賀循、侍中紀瞻、中書郎庾亮、大將軍諮議參軍梅陶、散騎郎張嶷等議，以：「肉刑之典，由來尚矣。 肇自古先，以及三代，聖哲明王所未曾改也。 豈是漢文常主所能易者乎！ 時蕭曹已沒，絳灌之徒不能正其義。 逮班固深論其事，以為外有輕刑之名，內實殺人。 又死刑太重，生刑太輕，生刑縱於上，死刑怨於下，輕重失當，故刑政不中也。 且原先王之造刑也，非以過怒也，非以殘人也，所以救奸，所以當罪。 今盜者竊人之財，淫者好人之色，亡者避叛之役，皆無殺害也，則加之以刑。 刑之則止，而加之斬戮，戮過其罪，死不可生，縱虐於此，歲以巨計。 此乃仁人君子所不忍聞，而況行之於政乎！ 若乃惑其名而不練其實，惡其生而趣其死，此畏水投舟，避坎蹈井，愚夫之不若，何取於政哉！ 今大晉中興，遵復古典，率由舊章，起千載之滯義，拯百殘之遺黎，使皇典廢而復存，黔首死而更生，至義暢於三代之際，遺風播乎百世之後，生肉枯骨，惠侔造化，豈不休哉！ 惑者乃曰，死猶不懲，而況于刑？ 然人者冥也，其至愚矣，雖加斬戮，忽為灰土，死事日往，生欲日存，未以為改。 若刑諸市朝，朝夕鑒戒，刑者詠為惡之永痛，惡者睹殘刖之長廢，故足懼也。 然後知先王之輕刑以禦物，顯誡以懲愚，其理遠矣。」
After enthronement, Wei Zhan as commandant argued: "Corporal mutilation was sage-approved; Emperor Wen abolished it and multiplied beheadings. The realm is bled white, yet law grows crueler—unlike Goujian's policy of cherishing the people. I urge restoring classical corporal punishment to build true peace. The court ordered a full debate. Wang Dao, He Xun, Ji Zhan, Yu Liang, Mei Tao, Zhang Ni, and others argued that mutilating penalties were ancient and venerable. From earliest kings through the three dynasties no wise ruler had changed them. They were not for a middling ruler like Emperor Wen to discard lightly. Xiao He and Cao Shen were dead; military men like Zhou Bo could not defend the reform. Ban Gu showed the reform only lightened the name while killing more. Death was too harsh, labor too soft; the living grew reckless, the condemned bitter—balance failed. Sages invented penalties not from spite or cruelty but to curb evil and fit the crime. Thieves, lechers, and deserters harm no life—mutilation could answer their guilt. Mutilation would end their crime, yet we add beheading—death outruns guilt, cannot be undone, and piles yearly by the thousands. Humane men cannot hear of it—how run a state on it? Chasing the label of "mercy" while ignoring reality is like fearing water and scuttling the boat—worse than folly. Restoring classical mutilation would revive sagely justice, redeem mutilated subjects, and heal the world—blessing rivaling heaven itself. Skeptics say death does not deter—why would cutting help? Men are blind to fear: execution becomes routine ash, lust for life returns—death does not reform them. Public mutilation shames the criminal and warns the crowd—true deterrence. Then men grasp why sages preferred "light" visible torture over hidden slaughter.
64
尚書令刁協、尚書薛兼等議，以為：「聖上悼殘荒之遺黎，傷犯死之繁眾，欲行刖以代死刑，使犯死之徒得存性命，則率土蒙更生之澤，兆庶必懷恩以反化也。 今中興祚隆，大命惟新，誠宜設寬法以育人。 然懼群小愚蔽，習玩所見而忽異聞，或未能咸服。 愚謂行刑之時，先明申法令，樂刑者刖，甘死者殺，則心必服矣。 古典刑不上大夫，今士人有犯者，謂宜如舊，不在刑例，則進退為允。」
Diao Xie and Xue Jian argued mutilation would spare capital convicts and win gratitude. The restored mandate calls for merciful nurture. Yet petty clerks might cling to habit and resist. Publish choice: accept mutilation or death—then men trust the process. Classical law spared high ministers; gentry offenders should likewise be exempt from mutilation for fairness.
65
尚書顗、郎曹彥、中書郎桓彝等議，以為：「復肉刑以代死，誠是聖王之至德，哀矜之弘私。 然竊以為刑罰輕重，隨時而作。 時人少罪而易威，則從輕而寬之； 時人多罪而難威，則宜化刑而濟之。 肉刑平世所應立，非救弊之宜也。 方今聖化草創，人有餘奸，習惡之徒，為非未已，截頭絞頸，尚不能禁，而乃更斷足劓鼻，輕其刑罰，使欲為惡者輕犯寬刑，蹈罪更眾，是為輕其刑以誘人於罪，殘其身以加楚酷也。 昔之畏死刑以為善人者，今皆犯輕刑而殘其身，畏重之常人，反為犯輕而致囚，此則何異斷刖常人以為恩仁邪！ 受刑者轉廣，而為非者日多，踴貴屨賤，有鼻者醜也。 徒有輕刑之名，而實開長惡之源。 不如以殺止殺，重以全輕，權小停之。 須聖化漸著，兆庶易威之日，徐施行也。」
Xun Yi, Cao Yan, Huan Yi, and others called mutilation the deepest mercy. Yet penalties must fit the age. When crime is rare, stay lenient; when crime spreads, shift methods to restore awe. Mutilation suits a tranquil age, not a broken one. Today villains still multiply under capital law; swapping to lighter mutilation would invite more crime, not less—tempting evil while scarring bodies. Men who once feared death would now risk mutilation; the law-abiding would stumble into light crimes—like amputating innocents and calling it kindness. Mutilation would spread while crime rose—like the proverb of pricey prosthetics and cheap shoes, a world of the noseless. You would gain a "lenient" label while feeding vice. Better to end crime with death for now, weight sparing the light, and shelve the plan. Wait until peace returns and the people fear authority again.
66
議奏，元帝猶欲從展所上。 大將軍王敦以為：「百姓習俗日久，忽復肉刑，必駭遠近。 且逆寇未殄，不宜有慘酷之聲，以聞天下。 」於是乃止。
The debate was filed; Prince Yuan still favored Wei Zhan. Wang Dun objected: long habit would panic the realm. With rebels still in the field, cruel reform would send the wrong signal. The plan was dropped.
67
咸康之世，庾冰好為糾察，近於繁細，後益矯違，復存寬縱，疏密自由，律令無用矣。
Under Yu Bing, justice veered from nitpicking to lax whim until law meant nothing.
68
至安帝元興末，桓玄輔政，又議欲復肉刑斬左右趾之法，以輕死刑，命百官議。 蔡廓上議曰：「建邦立法，弘教穆化，必隨時置制，德刑兼施。 長貞一以閑其邪，教禁以檢其慢，灑湛露以流潤，厲嚴霜以肅威，雖復質文迭用，而斯道莫革。 肉刑之設，肇自哲王。 蓋由曩世風淳，人多惇謹，圖像既陳，則機心直戢，刑人在塗，則不逞改操，故能勝殘去殺，化隆無為。 季末澆偽，設網彌密，利巧之懷日滋，恥畏之情轉寡。 終身劇役，不足止其奸，況乎黥劓，豈能反於善。 徒有酸慘之聲，而無濟俗之益。 至於棄市之條，實非不赦之罪，事非手殺，考律同歸，輕重均科，減降路塞，鐘陳以之抗言，元皇所為留湣。 今英輔翼贊，道邈伊周，誠宜明慎用刑，愛人弘育，申哀矜以革濫，移大辟于支體，全性命之至重，恢繁息於將來。 」而孔琳之議不同，用王朗、夏侯玄之旨。 時論多與琳之同，故遂不行。
At the end of Yuanxing (404–405), regent Huan Xuan revived debate on toe amputation to commute death. Cai Kuo wrote: founding a state requires laws that fit the hour, blending virtue and penalty. Hold one standard against vice, teach restraint, show mercy yet frost-like awe—form may shift, the principle never does. Mutilation began with sage founders. In a simple age pictorial law stilled guile; seeing the mutilated shamed the rash—so sages could "overcome cruelty" and reach effortless rule. A decadent age breeds clever evasion; denser nets only sharpen greed and dull shame. Lifetime labor cannot stop them—scar their faces and they will not turn good. You would hear only wailing, with no gain for morals. Market execution rules lump non-homicides with killers, blocking mercy—hence Zhong Chen remonstrated and Emperor Yuan stayed his hand. Under wise ministers greater than Yi Yin and the Duke of Zhou, use punishment sparingly, cherish life, curb excess, commute death to limb penalty where just, and spare the people. Kong Linzhi dissented, taking Wang Lang and Xiahou Xuan's line. Most court opinion sided with Kong Linzhi, so the measure died.
